article.body_html:
The bike has stopped, and a mechanic at the roadside offers to fix it for a small fee. It is convenient, but the bike is not yours: someone else owns it, someone else may be responsible for its repair, and you will be the one explaining the work afterwards. Before you say yes, three questions need an answer. Do you know what is wrong? Do you know the price? And does the shop know? Here is what to do first and what to ask.

Stop, make it safe, then decide

Move the bike out of traffic, switch off the engine and take photographs of the bike, the fault if you can see it, and the place. The mechanic's offer can wait for two minutes; your safety and the record cannot. Thuê xe máy Nguyễn Hà is open 09:00–21:00 daily, so during those hours call 0334 699 969 before any work starts. Outside those hours do not count on an answer: make yourself and the bike safe where it stands (off the road, locked, photographed) and leave any repair until you have spoken to the shop.

What to ask the mechanic

  1. What exactly is wrong? Ask to be shown, not just told.
  2. What exactly will you do, and will any part be replaced?
  3. What is the full price, including any part, before you begin?
  4. How long will it take?
  5. Can I keep any part you remove, and can I have a receipt or a written price?
  6. Can I photograph the work and the repaired part?

Agree the price before the work. A figure that appears afterwards, once the bike is in pieces, is a bad position to negotiate from. If the answer to the first question is vague, that is information too.

Three offers you may hear, and a calm answer to each

  • "Five minutes and it is fixed." Ask what the five minutes consist of and what it costs, then wait for the answer before you hand over the bike.
  • "This part is finished, it must be replaced." Ask to see the part and why it is finished, ask for the price of the part and the labour separately, and say you need to call the owner first.
  • "Come to my workshop." Ask how far it is and whether the bike can be ridden there safely. If it cannot, a bike pushed or carried to an unknown place is a bike the shop does not know the location of. Do not hand over the keys or let the bike leave your sight until the shop knows where it is going.

Two short Vietnamese phrases are enough for most of this: Sửa hết bao nhiêu tiền ạ? means "How much is the whole repair?", and Cho tôi xem chỗ hỏng với means "Please show me the fault". Asking them out loud before the work starts shows that you expect a price and an explanation.

What to ask the shop

When you reach the shop, ask three things in this order:

  • Do you want the bike repaired here, or do you prefer to arrange help?
  • If I use a roadside mechanic, who pays, and what do you need from me: the receipt, the photographs, the old part?
  • Is there a workshop you prefer, or any work you do not want done by anyone else?

Whether a roadside repair is refunded or refused is for the shop to say, so do not assume either. Ask, and keep the answer in writing if the shop uses messages. A Rental Motorbike Service Appointment: Agree Who Pays Before Work Begins covers the same question for planned work.

Whose decision is the repair?

Some jobs are small and visible, such as pumping up a tyre. Others change how the bike behaves: brakes, steering, wheels and anything inside the engine. Ask the shop before anyone touches those, or replaces any part, and do not ride a bike whose brakes or steering you do not trust. If the mechanic suggests that "everything needs changing", stop and call before agreeing to any of it.

Keep a cost log

ItemQuoted pricePaidPhoto or receipt
Work doneAgreed before the workAmount and timeOf the bike, the part and the receipt
Part replaced, if anyAgreed before the workAmount and timeOf the old and new part
Who did the workName or stall, place, phone numberNot applicableOf the stall and its sign

Fill the log in at the roadside, not that evening. A table with three rows is enough; what matters is that the price in the log is the price you agreed before the work started.

After the repair

Test the bike gently before you ride on: squeeze both brakes, check the lights and listen for new noises. Then send the shop the photographs, the receipt and the time, and ask how it wants the cost handled. Rental Motorbike Puncture in Hanoi: Where to Stop and What to Record covers a flat tyre in more detail, and the information to send the shop when a scooter will not start lists what to note. You can reach the shop through its contact page, and the Breakdowns & Roadside Help category has the other guides for when a bike stops.
